name: Jupiter satellites tracked
summary: Galileo tracked four points of light near Jupiter night after night and concluded they were moons circling it, showing not everything in the sky orbits Earth.
description: Repeated telescopic positions of objects near Jupiter, interpreted as four bodies revolving around it rather than fixed stars.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.

market.note: Commercial availability is not a milestone of a scientific knowledge result.

date.label: Jan. 1610
date.basis: Dated observations begin 7 January; four objects are recorded on 13 January; interpretation follows the changing positions.

events.statement: Repeated telescopic positions of objects near Jupiter, interpreted as four bodies revolving around it rather than fixed stars.
events.caveats: Priority disputes with other observers are not resolved here; the result alone does not distinguish every geocentric, geoheliocentric and heliocentric system.

evidence.locator: Original fols.17r–18v; translation printed pp. 36–39 (PDF pp. 37–40)
evidence.supports: Records instrument dependence, successive dated positions, orbital inference and four objects on 13 January.
Confirms the 7 January and 13 January observing dates.

events.statement: Kepler responded to Galileo’s published account and discussed four bodies in the vicinity of Jupiter and their motions.
events.caveats: Kepler had not yet independently confirmed the discoveries with an equivalent telescope; agreement was not universal. Receipt by Galileo or a wider correspondence is not established by the date of Kepler’s signed letter.

evidence.locator: Dissertatio, discussions of the four Jovian planets and concluding dated letter
evidence.supports: The dated response engages directly with Galileo’s specific claim.

links.statement: An improved instrument let Galileo see objects near Jupiter that weaker instruments had not revealed; repeated observations supported the satellite interpretation.
links.scope: Padua, January 1610; the recorded Jovian observations.
links.alternatives: Different adequate telescopes and independent observers were alternatives.
links.caveats: The instrument enabled visual evidence; changing positions over nights supplied the inference.
links.timing: The suitable improved instrument was already in use on 7 January within the development interval; publication followed in March.
